$comment: An element of a task, and the thing that actually appears in a queue, a backlog, or a plan as a trackable entry. Something becomes a work-item at the moment somebody judges it actionable and commits it to the system: raw input — an idea, a request, a problem noticed — turns into a work-item when someone decides this needs doing. A work-item is either a work-unit, which is atomic, or a workflow, which is a composition of further work-items. That makes it a recursive type: a workflow is itself a work-item, so a task can hold atoms and compounds at any depth. A work-item is NOT a task. A task is the planning-level container and may hold several; a work-item is the individual entry. In simple cases a task holds exactly one and the two look identical, which is why they are used interchangeably and should not be.

name.$comment: What the work-item is called, as it is said. Stated as what to do.

kind.$comment: Atomic or composite. A work-unit is fully specified — what goes in, what operation is performed, what comes out, and every parameter bound — and cannot be broken down further without ceasing to be one operation producing one output. A workflow is a structured composition of further work-items, and is itself a work-item.

actions.$comment: The actions it is made of. One or more: a work-item that comes to no action is an entry in a backlog and nothing else.

work-items.$comment: The work-items composed, where this is a workflow. The recursion lives here — each is a work-item in its own right, atomic or composite.

allOf.$comment: A workflow is a composition, so it must say what it composes. A work-unit is atomic, so it must not.

$comment-absences: No worker or assignee: who does it belongs to the dispatch. No status: whether it is open, underway or finished is a readout over its actions, and a work-item that could assert its own completion is marking its own homework. The corpus's older note lists a status as intrinsic; that was written before the goal moved onto the task, and is not followed here.
